home.headline: Speak instead of typing
home.lead: Murmel turns your voice into text — wherever the cursor happens to be.
home.how: Press the key, speak, let go. The text appears where you meant to write anyway: in the editor, in the chat window, in the address bar. No window gets in the way, no copying and pasting.
home.privacy: Speech recognition runs entirely on this machine. The model is downloaded once and works without internet afterwards. No account, no subscription, no recording that ends up on someone else's server.
home.refinement: If you like, a second key tidies the text up as it goes: filler words out, punctuation in, phrased as an email or as notes. That too stays on this machine, as long as you use a language model running here.

dictionary.title: Dictionary
dictionary.description: Names, technical terms, product names — anything Murmel keeps spelling differently than you mean it. Enter only the correct spelling; what arrived instead does not need to be listed.
dictionary.empty: No entries yet. Add words that are frequently misrecognised.
dictionary.hint: An empty entry is dropped when saving.
dictionary.howBefore: On Whisper models the list is handed to the speech model before it listens. It then expects these words and often spells them right on its own; the comparison below is skipped in that case.
dictionary.howAfter: On every other model — and whenever a Whisper model gets it wrong anyway — Murmel compares each word in the result against your entries: by spelling, and for words without accented characters also by sound. Close enough, and it is replaced. That is why the correct entry is enough: you never have to collect the wrong variants.
dictionary.howPhrases: A phrase is an entry containing spaces, such as "Silly Tavern". Murmel considers up to three consecutive words at a time, so "Charge B" becomes "ChargeBee" and words the recogniser split apart find each other again.
dictionary.howLimits: Accented characters are carried along: "Grüße" is found even when "gruesse" arrived. What is not supported are scripts written without spaces between words, such as Chinese or Japanese — there is no way to tell where a word ends.
